Q: Type casting char pointer to be of type struct pointer A:

To focus on the question in your title: You can cast an array of char or unsigned char¹ to any other type, so long as the buffer has at least the right size and at least the right alignment. (An array of signed char would work too, but no one ever does that.) You may want to consistently use char buffers to hold strings and unsigned char for bytes of untyped data.

C always counts object sizes as a number of char (even on machines that can address individual bits). This means that, to fill a buffer with any larger object, you need to increment it by the size of the object. And EVENT_SIZE is defined to be sizeof (struct inotify_event). In this case, it appears that an inotify_event struct can contain bytes of extra data at the end, and that how many is stored in its len field. That appears to be the reason why the loop is filling an array of char instead of struct inotify_event, and why it increments the current position by EVENT_SIZE + event.len.

Language-Lawyery Update

Although this is a bit more into the weeds than you need right now, I have to address it. There are a number of incorrect answers and comments claiming that there is some kind of undefined behavior from strict aliasing. The C23 Standard §6.5.4(6) says (adding emphasis to the clauses relevant to your example, which are not about objects of no declared type):

If a value is copied into an object having no declared type using memcpy or memmove, or is copied as an array of character type, then the effective type of the modified object for that access and for subsequent accesses that do not modify the value is the effective type of the object from which the value is copied, if it has one. For all other accesses to an object having no declared type, the effective type of the object is simply the type of the lvalue used for the access.

The clause “or is copied as an array of character type” is clearly intended to parallel “copied into an object having no declared type” rather than “using memcpy or memmove”, as the reading “*If a value is copied into an object having no declared type is copied as an array of character type” makes no grammatical or logical sense.

Since this code sample copies the struct as an array of character type, the effective type is set correctly, and the pointer alias is legal (next paragraph, first item). There is one other potential source of undefined behavior: casting a misaligned pointer is undefined behavior. I don’t think this would be an issue with this type, but it is in general safer to declare a buffer you will use to store some other type of data with alignas or _Alignas.

Even if a compiler that didn’t allow this very common idiom could declare itself conforming to some people’s interpretation of the language standard, no actual compiler does and any compiler that did would break on a lot of existing code, so it’s nothing you need to worry about.

Copying with memcpy() will work in more cases and perform as well, so it’s good advice.

It's quick to type and it will upgrade Chocolatey and everything else.

Q: postgresql return 0 if returned value is null A:

Use coalesce

COALESCE(value [, ...])

The COALESCE function returns the first of its arguments that is not null.
Null is returned only if all arguments are null. It is often used to substitute a default value for null values when data is retrieved for display.

Edit

Here's an example of COALESCE with your query:

SELECT AVG( price )
FROM(
      SELECT *, cume_dist() OVER ( ORDER BY price DESC ) FROM web_price_scan
      WHERE listing_Type = 'AARM'
        AND u_kbalikepartnumbers_id = 1000307
        AND ( EXTRACT( DAY FROM ( NOW() - dateEnded ) ) ) * 24 < 48
        AND COALESCE( price, 0 ) > ( SELECT AVG( COALESCE( price, 0 ) )* 0.50
                                     FROM ( SELECT *, cume_dist() OVER ( ORDER BY price DESC )
                                           FROM web_price_scan
                                           WHERE listing_Type='AARM'
                                             AND u_kbalikepartnumbers_id = 1000307
                                             AND ( EXTRACT( DAY FROM ( NOW() - dateEnded ) ) ) * 24 < 48
                                         ) g
                                    WHERE cume_dist < 0.50
                                  )
        AND COALESCE( price, 0 ) < ( SELECT AVG( COALESCE( price, 0 ) ) *2
                                     FROM( SELECT *, cume_dist() OVER ( ORDER BY price desc )
                                           FROM web_price_scan
                                           WHERE listing_Type='AARM'
                                             AND u_kbalikepartnumbers_id = 1000307
                                             AND ( EXTRACT( DAY FROM ( NOW() - dateEnded ) ) ) * 24 < 48
                                         ) d
                                     WHERE cume_dist < 0.50)
     )s
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5

IMHO COALESCE should not be use with AVG because it modifies the value. NULL means unknown and nothing else. It's not like using it in SUM. In this example, if we replace AVG by SUM, the result is not distorted. Adding 0 to a sum doesn't hurt anyone but calculating an average with 0 for the unknown values, you don't get the real average.

In that case, I would add price IS NOT NULL in WHERE clause to avoid these unknown values.

Q: Using numpy.isin for set operations where set members are Vectors or Matrices A:

as far as I'm aware that does not exist in numpy. If you want to check if an array of shape (15, 8) is in x, you could do something like this:

def isin_axis0(element, collection):
    return np.any(np.all(element == collection, axis=(1, 2))

Then,

>>> isin_axis0(x[0], x)
True

>>> isin_axis0(np.random.rand(15, 8), x)
False

This is just a bruteforce solution though, no clever trick. It checks every value in element against every value in the same row/column in collection to see if they are equal. Then, if every value if equal for one matrix or more, it returns True. Otherwise, it returns False.
